newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians angry but violence not likely.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians angry but violence not likely.

text.p: The crisis facing Israeli-PLO peace moves may have plunged Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza into gloom but analysts say the frustrations are not likely to explode into a fresh round of violence.

Officials in Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority, angry at Israel's decision to build a new Jewish settlement in Jerusalem, have been further enraged by Israel's decision to withdraw from only a tiny area of the West Bank.

"It is a real crisis but I do not think it will finish the peace process because neither side has enough power to do that. The peace process is stronger than both sides," said Ghassan al-Khatib, a former member of the Palestinian team negotiating with Israel.
"It may also lead to tension on the street, but not to the extent to destroy the peace process," he said.

Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died during gun battles and stone-throwing demonstrations in September that were sparked by Israel's opening of a tunnel near Islamic holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem.
All the hallmarks of the tension that ignited September's violence were once again visible across the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Palestinian newspapers are full of stories of Israeli land seizures, demolition of Arab-owned houses in areas still under Israeli jurisdiction and settlement expansion.

Israel's decision to build 6,500 homes for Jews at the southern edge of Jerusalem has already sparked peaceful demonstrations, where Palestinian officials struggled to prevent young Arabs clashing with Israeli soldiers.
However, many fear an explosion of anger once Israeli bulldozers start work on the pine-covered hill.
Palestinian officials, including Arafat, have accused Israel of cheating on the implementation of self-rule deals. Some have even warned that Israeli policies were inviting violence.

"Israel is compiling provocations, compiling measures by confiscating land, building settlements, withdrawing residency cards and closing Palestinian institutions," Faisal al-Husseini, the top PLO official in Jerusalem warned in an interview with the Voice of Palestine radio station on Tuesday.
"It seems that there is an Israeli stand to drive matters to a crisis and I am afraid that this is what may come," he said.
Israel, who Palestinians say has been training military units to enter self-ruled cities in case of trouble, has warned it will crush any violence.
But Khatib said that Palestinian anger, while genuine, appeared aimed at inviting international pressure on Israel to change its policies.
PLO officials say the Palestinian leadership intends to besiege Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu diplomatically rather than direct Palestinians towards violence.
"The crisis this time is no less than the crisis in September," Khatib said.
"But the street reaction is much more restrained. I think that the Palestinian leadership want to draw international pressure on Israel to alter its stands," he said.
